doc.title: Ralph Humphrey interviewed by Monk Rowe, Toronto, Canada, January 11, 2003

title: Choosing music, student deferments and cheap college
summary: Humphrey wanted music as a career, pursued a teaching credential, and stayed in school, which deferred Vietnam service; they talk about the fairness of deferments and cheap tuition.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: When was it that you thought hmm, maybe there’s a career in music for me?

Well in high school I was definitely in love with playing the drums and playing every kind of music I could and playing outside and doing little gigs and having just a great time. But I didn’t really know what kind of a career I could have. I went to college, continued studying, became a music major, continually being turned on by musicians in the Bay Area, by music I was hearing, by records that I was listening to, by great instructors. And it got me more involved with wanting to play music as a career but I really didn’t know how I was going to do it. So I was playing it safe and I was going for a teacher’s credential so I was getting my five years and doing the whole thing. And it did keep me out of going to Vietnam, because it was that time.
A student deferment and then it was a marriage deferment and then it was getting a child deferment. So yes. But you had to stay in school and take a full load for the entire time otherwise you were—
You know when you look back on that now, because I was in on that a little bit later but I recall watching the draft where they are picking out the numbers. Did you —

That was before the lottery. So at that time they were drafting and if you were say out of school and draft age and healthy, they wanted you. It wasn’t necessarily a conscious thing of avoiding the draft it was just that I knew that school was important and that this was certainly one way that I could defer any service. So staying in school, which was very important to me, I did so and luckily I was able to get to a point where it was past the point where they were drafting.
Right. When you look back on that time do you think the student deferment was a fair thing?
Yeah. Well the people that let’s say couldn’t afford to be in college.
They probably didn’t think it was fair.
College was very cheap. I put myself through college just by playing gigs and whatnot. It’s so different than nowadays. I mean really when you think about it, the state college was—
I got great instruction, I didn’t have to leave my neighborhood to get great instruction.
Yeah we thought it was a big deal to take out a loan for two thousand dollars.
Oh I know, exactly. So I think everybody had the benefit if they wanted, to go to school, to get a higher education.
